primary_topics: Closing remarks at the First Pacific-MVP Group Corporate Governance Enhancement Session on 'Navigating the New World of Business,' November 19, 2012 -- thanking Professor Thomas Donaldson of the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania for his presentation

The substantive lessons from Donaldson's presentation: managing operational risks (strategy + luck: two lions, deer); paying for peril (borrowing short on fluctuating rates, lending long on fixed rates); mesmerizing goals; the parable of the shadu; too many regulations penalize the law-abiding

CJP's personal thanks to Manuel V. Pangilinan for the opportunity to serve as an independent director in the First Pacific Group -- citing the high standards of ethics and corporate governance that characterize its undertakings
sub_topics: Professor Donaldson's key teachings summarized in the closing remarks: (1) managing operational risks is a matter of strategy, though sometimes luck helps (two lions who happened to be in the right place when a deer fatally bumped its head on a tree); (2) it is not enough to be formidable and profitable -- equally important to be values-based and ethics-oriented; (3) we are not just pursuing business to make money but evolving a corporate culture reflecting convictions and principles; (4) even well-intentioned individuals and companies can stumble when 'dangerous currents like mesmerizing goals haunt us'; (5) tenacious adherence to ethics is the 'real and ultimate source of strength as we navigate the huge ocean of business'

Blame-and-legislation reaction: 'the response to failures is to point fingers and to blame others... the knee-jerk reaction is to pass legislation and create new regulations'; but too many regulations 'penalize the law-abiding and make it more difficult for them to recover and to succeed'

Laws' limitation: 'Laws tend to punish past wrongdoings; they rarely address future witchcraft of the unethical and the undisciplined. For lawbreakers do not care; they simply invent new ways to steal, to beguile and to metamorphose because they know that no law and no regulation is perfect.'

Philippine pyramiding scams: just a few days ago, authorities stumbled on another scam that 'vowed incredible 50 percent rewards monthly, only to encourage the hapless victims to reinvest and eventually to lose both their principals and earnings'
Lehman Brothers and AIG: triple-A rated companies whose collapse triggered the 2008 global financial crisis; similar schemes exist in the Philippines

Paying for peril: 'the phenomenon of rewarding short and suffering long'; entities that borrow short-term on fluctuating rates and lend long-term on fixed rates will 'never stabilize and will always be at risk'

Personal thanks to Manuel Pangilinan: 'as someone who is used to working in an environment of independence and integrity, I have found fulfillment and contentment in the high standards of ethics and corporate governance that characterize our undertakings in the First Pacific Group'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered November 19, 2012 as closing remarks at the First Pacific-MVP Group Corporate Governance Enhancement Session on 'Navigating the New World of Business,' this address by CJP thanks Professor Thomas Donaldson of the Wharton School for his 'illuminating presentation.' He synthesizes Donaldson's key lessons: managing operational risks is a matter of strategy, 'although sometimes luck helps' (two lions who happened to be in the right place when a deer fatally bumped its head on a tree); being formidable and profitable is not enough -- equally important to be 'values-based and ethics-oriented'; corporate culture should reflect convictions and principles, not just profit-seeking; even well-intentioned companies stumble when 'dangerous currents like mesmerizing goals haunt us'; 'tenacious adherence to ethics is our real and ultimate source of strength.' He applies Donaldson's lessons to Philippine realities: the 2008 Lehman Brothers/AIG collapse mirrors local pyramiding scams vowing '50 percent rewards monthly' ('when something is too good to be true, it is indeed never good and never true'); the parable of the shadu (pointing fingers at failures) and the knee-jerk legislative response are both wrong -- 'too many regulations penalize the law-abiding; laws tend to punish past wrongdoings but rarely address future witchcraft of the unethical because lawbreakers simply invent new ways to steal.' Donaldson's concept of 'paying for peril' (borrowing short on fluctuating rates, lending long on fixed rates) explains why such entities 'will never stabilize and will always be at risk.' He closes with personal thanks to Manuel V. Pangilinan for 'giving me the opportunity to be an independent director in some of the leading companies of this conglomerate; as a retired jurist used to working in an environment of independence and integrity, I have found fulfillment and contentment in the high standards of ethics and corporate governance that characterize our undertakings in the First Pacific Group.'
